retrieval_text: A 2-year-old female child, third in birth order, born to parents who are first cousins, delivered vaginally at term without complications, presented with sparse scalp hair, absent body hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes, and delayed tooth eruption. The mother reported that the child does not sweat and has had recurrent fevers since the neonatal period. Psychomotor development was normal. There was no family history of similar symptoms, except for a previous female sibling with similar complaints and a distinctive appearance, who experienced recurrent fever and chest infections during the neonatal period and died at 6 months of age. The parents' first pregnancy ended in a miscarriage at 2 months for unknown reasons. Skin examination showed smooth, normal-looking skin with normal palmoplantar skin and dermatoglyphics. The child had an aged appearance with finely wrinkled skin around the eyes, an everted lower lip, and low-set ears. Scalp hair was sparse, light-colored, and thin, with complete absence of eyelashes, eyebrows, and body hair. Oral examination revealed only two conical, widely spaced maxillary teeth and a low-arched, flat palate. Nails were normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities, and there was no evidence of mental retardation.
A 30-year-old male arrived at the emergency department experiencing shortness of breath, coughing, production of phlegm, fever, and night sweats for approximately one month.

A 4-year-old male child presented with discolored teeth. His medical history was unremarkable. The mother reported an uncomplicated, full-term pregnancy from a nonconsanguineous marriage. The child appeared well-nourished with a height of 96.25 cm. Parents noted normal mental development. The child had sparse, discolored hair and had undergone 3-4 haircuts. He had a broad forehead, prominent in lateral view, with a head circumference of 51.25 cm, within the 50th percentile. There was no splitting of the superficial layer of fingernails or toenails. Dental examination showed the eruption of all four permanent first molars. Primary teeth had been extracted due to dental abscess formation. The remaining primary teeth were opaque and yellowish-brown, with severe attrition of mandibular primary incisors and maxillary primary canines. Pulp chambers of maxillary and mandibular primary canines were visible through the thin enamel. Both posterior and anterior occlusal relationships indicated a Class III tendency.

A 12-year-old male with no notable birth or medical history presented with concerns about lower abdominal distention and had reduced his food intake over the past 3 months. He engaged in excessive exercise relative to his food intake. Despite significant weight loss, he expressed concerns about his abdominal size. During the initial consultation, he was observed to be very lean with a body mass index (BMI) of 11.5 kg/m2 and had a heart rate of approximately 40 beats/min, indicating sinus bradycardia. Enteral nutritional supplements were administered to improve his weight. Seven days after the first visit, he was emergently hospitalized due to disorientation. On admission, his height was 145 cm, weight was 20.9 kg (BMI: 9.9 kg/m2), and he presented with impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) E3V4M6), bradycardia (heart rate ~40 beats/min), and slow breathing (respiratory rate ~10 cycles/min).
A 66-year-old multiparous female patient presented with recurrent vaginal bleeding and dull lower abdominal pain for 2 months.
A 55-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of severe fatigue, diarrhea, and vomiting.

A 66-year-old retired male patient visited the pain clinic in mid-2014 with complaints of episodic headaches over the past 10 years. These headaches occurred up to 8 times daily, beginning as a sharp pain near the right eye and spreading to the right side of the face, vertex, and upper back of the head. Each episode lasted between 45 and 75 minutes, with pain-free intervals in between. The pain was described as intense and unbearable, accompanied by rhinorrhea in the right nostril and conjunctival injection in the right eye without swelling. The patient experienced significant restlessness during these episodes. Treatment with a greater occipital nerve block using 40 mg methylprednisolone and 20 mg bupivacaine provided complete pain relief within minutes, lasting for 12 months. This treatment was repeated twice, each time offering 6 months of relief. By mid-2016, the headaches had subsided, and the patient remained headache-free for 2.5 years. His medical history included an abdominal aortic aneurysm surgery, and his family history was unremarkable. In July 2019, the patient returned to the clinic with a new, constant stabbing pain radiating from the back of the right side of his head to the right side of the vertex, forehead, right ear, and jaw, accompanied by numbness and paresthesias. He did not report neck pain. The right eye exhibited continuous tearing, conjunctival injection, and eyelid edema, along with excessive rhinorrhea. The patient felt particularly restless at night. His baseline pain score was 6 out of 10, with exacerbations reaching 9 out of 10, occurring 2-3 times daily and lasting 20-30 minutes, sometimes triggered by neck movements. Physical examination revealed mild tearing, conjunctival injection, and slight eyelid edema in the right eye, along with hyperesthesia over the right vertex and forehead. Neurological examination was otherwise normal. Passive neck extension was extremely limited and reproduced severe pain exacerbations. Palpation of the right SCM muscle elicited tenderness and exacerbated the referred pain. An injection of 30 mg of 1% lidocaine into the right SCM muscle resulted in a reduction of pain from a score of 7 out of 10 to 0 within 4 minutes. The numbness in the forehead and vertex disappeared, neck range of motion improved, and right-sided tearing and conjunctival injection began to subside, followed by resolving eyelid edema. Symptom relief lasted for 4 weeks before partially relapsing. In September 2019, the patient returned and received another injection, this time with 20 mg lidocaine and 10 mg bupivacaine, resulting in complete pain resolution for an additional 2 months.

A 32-year-old female presented with severe pain in the right temporomandibular joint (TMJ) region, right ear, limited mouth opening, and facial asymmetry. She was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without perinatal or notable postnatal issues. Her parents noticed progressive enlargement of her right cheek and differing eyelid width in the months following birth. The facial asymmetry became more pronounced over the years but has remained stable recently. No other family members are affected, and her mother reported a normal pregnancy. The enlargement extended from the midline to the preauricular region and down to the lower border of the mandible. The skin on the right side of the face appeared normal with no changes in thickness. Extraoral examination showed that the right side of the mandible was larger than the left. The outer contour of the right ear was slightly larger and differently shaped compared to the left ear. The nose was normal with no deviation, but the chin was deviated toward the right side. The lower lip on the right side appeared thicker with drooping at the corner of the mouth, and the lips on the right side were very dry. The patient reported clicking in the left TMJ, difficulty chewing, and headaches on the right side. Physical examination revealed a normal symmetric body and mental health. The mouth opening was 12 mm. Intraoral examination showed tongue asymmetry with unilateral enlargement of fungiform papillae on the right side. The teeth on the affected side appeared normal except for the maxillary right first molar, which was significantly larger than the maxillary left first molar. The lower right first molar was slightly larger than the lower left first molar. The lower dental centerline was deviated to the right, and there was a downward canting of the occlusal plane. Occlusal examination revealed unattainable central relation, early contact in both central occlusion and right lateral movement, and a discrepancy in the range of mandibular motion. The patient was referred for further evaluation.

A 21-year-old male with no previous history of illness presented with fever, a mild headache, body aches, joint pain, and a dry cough. These symptoms started four days prior to the presentation. It was only when he noticed a rash that he came to the hospital. He had immigrated from Asia five years prior. There was no recent international travel history. He recently returned from Tennessee five days prior to the presentation. However, he reported that he did not visit the densely forested areas. On examination, there was a maculopapular, blanching rash over the volar region of the forearm, lower leg, and over his body and neck. He reported no itching or pain over the rash. He had been taking NyQuil since the onset of the fever. Despite this, his temperature was 101°F during admission. On physical examination, his conjunctiva appeared mildly injected. Besides, there was nasal congestion and a sore throat. There was diffuse muscle tenderness and arthralgia. All other systems, including the neurological, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems, were unremarkable. Measles IgM was ordered, which came back negative.

A 12-year-old boy from the Northwest Gondar Amhara regional state presented with left flank swelling for the past 3 months. Three days prior to admission, he began experiencing pain in the left flank, accompanied by high-grade fever, chills, rigor, and vomiting. He did not report any urinary or respiratory symptoms. His maternal pregnancy course and medical history were unremarkable, and he was born at a health center. His past medical history was also unremarkable. He has seven siblings, none of whom exhibited similar symptoms. His mother had no history of radiation exposure, use of traditional medicine, or chemotherapy during pregnancy. No dysmorphisms were observed in his general appearance. Vital signs were as follows: pulse rate 142 beats/min, respiratory rate 33 breaths/min, temperature 38.5 °C, and blood pressure 105/65 mmHg. Anthropometric measurements indicated severe stunting. Abdominal examination revealed a distended abdomen, asymmetry with bulging on the left flank, a visible horizontal line, an upward umbilical slit, and absent rectus abdominis muscles. The abdomen was soft with a tender cystic mass on the left flank, measuring 13 × 11 cm, palpable bimanually. Both testes were undescended. The patient also had scoliosis and developmental dysplasia of the hips with a waddling gait. Urinary analysis showed many red blood cells and positive leukocyte esterase. Renal function tests were normal with a creatinine level of 0.72 mg/dl and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 44 mg/dl. Hemoglobin was normal at 12.7 gm/dl, and electrolyte levels were normal.
An 11-year-old male presented with muscle pain, weakness, lack of appetite, and vomiting.
A 76-year-old male with a history of hypertension managed with anti-hypertensive medication experienced a sudden, painless decrease in vision in the left eye (OS) for one day.

A twenty-four-year-old female with a lifelong history of epilepsy and cognitive impairment presented with cyclic episodes of lethargy and behavioral changes. She had a history of intrauterine toxoplasmosis infection, resulting in colpocephaly, absence of posterior hemispheric structures, bilateral parieto-occipital porencephaly, and malformation of the right frontal lobe. Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, including an absent splenium, was also noted. Developmental delays were observed during childhood, and seizures began at age 5, with multiple seizure types including atonic and generalized tonic-clonic. Approximately two years prior to presenting to Mayo Clinic, she began experiencing episodes of hypothermia with temperatures as low as 30.5°C, systemic hypotension, lethargy, and compromised functional status, leading to hospitalization for breakthrough seizures. During these episodes, she was consistently hyponatremic. These episodes occurred monthly and resolved over one to two weeks. Over the course of two years, she was found to be thrombocytopenic, anemic, and occasionally leukopenic. These hematological changes were initially attributed to valproic acid, which was part of her antiepileptic regimen along with lamotrigine for fifteen years. Valproic acid was discontinued in January 2012, and she was switched to levetiracetam, but her blood counts continued to decline. After discontinuing levetiracetam, her seizures were managed with zonisamide, clobazam, and rufinamide, and a vagal nerve stimulator was placed. Despite these changes, her blood counts remained depressed during subsequent hospitalizations. During a recent episode of lethargy and poor responsiveness, she was admitted to her local hospital and transferred to our institution.

The patient is a 17-year-old female presenting with proximal muscle weakness since early childhood. She is the second child of healthy, nonconsanguineous Russian parents. Her pregnancy and delivery were normal, with a birth weight of 3.80 kg and length of 52 cm.

A 63-year-old male patient presented with a painful swelling on the inside of the right cheek, which had been increasing in size over the past month. He reported no history of jaw cysts. Clinical examination identified a firm, mobile nodule on the right buccal mucosa, just anterior to the ramus mandibulae, measuring 2.5 cm in diameter. The overlying mucosa was intact.

A 4-year-old boy was admitted with complaints of hard skin for over 3 years, unclear vision, and communication difficulties for one day. He was born weighing 3 kg and appeared normal at birth but soon exhibited failure to thrive. At one month old, his skin became swollen and sclerodermatous on the trunk, and he experienced loss of scalp hair and stunted growth. Prior to admission, he had blurred vision, communication difficulties, dull eyes, and an inability to speak. Physical examination revealed distinctive facial features, including prominent eyes and scalp veins, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, generalized alopecia with sparse downy hairs, a narrow nasal bridge, thin lips, micrognathia, and small ear lobes. His neck was soft, Brinell's sign was negative, Klinefelter's sign was negative, Babbitt's sign was positive bilaterally, tendon reflexes were present, limb muscle strength was grade IV, muscle tension was high, and his skin was stiff with poor elasticity and extensive mottled pigmentation on the trunk. He had bilateral metacarpophalangeal joint contracture deformity, flexion deformity of both proximal knuckles, difficulty squatting, and fixed hip and knee joint contractures, with a horse-riding posture. He measured 77 cm in height (<1st percentile) and weighed 7.8 kg (<1st percentile). He was unable to speak or communicate and was too young for a detailed ophthalmic examination.

A 13-year-old male was admitted due to progressive difficulty in walking and clumsiness, first noticed by his mother around the age of 5. His birth history and early neurodevelopment until 1 year of age were normal. He achieved head control at 3 months, rolled over at 5 months, and sat independently at 10 months. Subsequent developmental milestones were delayed: standing with support at 16 months and walking independently at 21 months. He spoke his first meaningful words at 2 years, formed phrases at 4 years, and constructed simple sentences by 5 years. At 5 years old, his mother observed a slow, broad-based gait and generalized weakness in his movements, but no medical consultation was sought at that time. His walking difficulties gradually worsened, and he recently experienced challenges in academic performance. The patient has one sister. His father died in a car accident at age 40. There is no family history of neurological disorders or renal stones. On admission, physical examination revealed minor dysmorphic features, including a long face, macrognathia, high arched palate, and large ears. Neurological examination showed mild higher cortical dysfunction, dysarthria, upper limb and gait ataxia, hyperreflexia with bilateral extensor toe signs. Motor power and muscle tone were normal. Sensory examination was normal except for impaired vibration and position sense in the lower extremities. Cranial nerve functions were intact, and optic fundi appeared normal. There were no tremors or involuntary movements.

A 30-year-old Jamaican-American male presented with one month of bilateral foot pain and ulcerations, with severe pain on the bottom of his left foot. He was active-duty military and a former professional athlete with no significant past medical history. He reported numbness on the plantar surface of both feet, which progressed to pain, worse at night and unrelieved by compression and over-the-counter pain medications. Physical examination revealed intact vibratory sensation in the lower extremities, extreme tenderness to palpation on the left foot, decreased dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of both feet, and decreased sensation on the plantar surface of the left foot. After a trial of compression stockings, ibuprofen, and acetaminophen, he presented to the emergency department with worsening foot pain.

A 14-year-old male presented with a 5-year history of a non-painful, protruding mass located in the right preauricular area. Physical examination identified a firm, dome-shaped mass measuring 1.5 cm in diameter, which was attached to the overlying skin but did not cause any skin changes. The entire mass was excised under local anesthesia. Upon gross examination, the mass appeared reddish-brown, globular, and had a stony hard consistency.

A 22-year-old male from Nepal experienced intermittent nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and breathlessness over the past two months. These symptoms worsened in the last 10 days, accompanied by facial puffiness, pedal edema, decreased urine output, and continued breathlessness. He reported no orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, seizures, hematuria, pyuria, or lithuria. There was no family history of similar conditions.
